The system-level aspects of AV fleets delivering public mobility include not only the maturation of AV technology but also the challenges of vehicle electrification and managing and coordinating multiple AV fleets to safely and efficiently deliver on-demand mobility services. High-level conclusions and insights for an AMD network system in the mid- to near futures (5 to 10 years) drawn from the composite of the Phases I, II, and III research—with a sampling of the most significant findings—are presented next. Selected Phase III Research Findings 1. A system-of-systems view and approach is required to achieve the full vision of effective, safe, and efficient public mobility using AV fleets, including appropriate jurisdictional authority for management and monitoring of the AMD network transport system. Interface points—both digital multidirectional communications and physical infrastructure, such as stations, to facilitate transfer between complementary modes—will be critical. 2. Intelligent roadway infrastructure can enhance the safety and throughput capacity of AV systems at roadway intersections and stations/curbfronts. Drawing on established principles from automated train control and emerging cooperative driving automation for roadways, IRI enhances the perception of AVs while providing the management authority with independent observability of various modes and their operational performance, enhances the safety and operations of traditional (nonautomated) modes, and offers pedestrians, micromobility, and vulnerable road users additional safety benefits. Although originally introduced to enhance roadway intersection safety, IRI is equally critical to protect passengers in the boarding process at high-capacity stations. Drawing on recent deployment experience, IRI may be equally critical in documenting AV performance and adherence to policy as an independent validator. This is explored more in Phase IV research. 3. Electrification of AV fleets will present significant operational and cost impacts.
